subject: geography
title: Earthquakes: Shaking the Ground
welcome_lead: Feel the ground tremble! Today you'll learn how earthquakes happen, how they are measured, and why some shake more than others.
meta_desc: KS3 Geography adventure on earthquakes, the Richter scale, focus and epicentre.
final_note: Excellent! You can now describe how earthquakes are measured and located.

concepts.def: Sudden shaking of Earth's crust from plate movement.
Point underground where the quake starts.
Point on surface directly above the focus.
Smaller quake following the main one.

walkthroughs.body_html: When plates push or grind, pressure builds in the rocks. Eventually they snap, releasing energy as seismic waves.
The focus is the underground starting point. The epicentre is the point on the surface directly above it, where shaking is usually strongest.
The Richter scale measures magnitude. Each step up means about 10 times more shaking. A 7.0 is far stronger than a 5.0!

options: The surface point above the focus
The deepest point in the ocean
The hottest part of Earth
A type of volcano
Ground shaking
Rainfall
Wind speed
Temperature

mcqs.q: Why does oceanic crust subduct beneath continental crust?
options: Oceanic crust subducts because the ocean pushes it down with its weight.
Oceanic crust is denser (basaltic) than continental crust (granitic), so when they collide the denser oceanic plate sinks into the mantle, forming a trench and volcanic arc.
Humans affect the carbon cycle by eating plants.
Continental crust subducts because it is thicker and heavier.

mcqs.q: How do humans affect the carbon cycle?
options: Humans affect the carbon cycle by eating plants.
Humans only affect the carbon cycle by breathing out CO2.
By burning fossil fuels (releasing stored geological carbon to the atmosphere) and deforestation (reducing the biosphere store and releasing carbon).
Continental crust subducts because it is thicker and heavier.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary data in geography fieldwork?
options: Primary data is collected in primary schools and secondary data in secondary schools.
Primary data is collected first-hand by the researcher (surveys, measurements, observations); secondary data already exists and is found in sources (census data, maps, published reports).
Primary data is more important and secondary data is less reliable.
Humans affect the carbon cycle by eating plants.
